article: Does haddock have more vitamin B12 than cod?
Compare matching cooked portions and see how much each fish contributes to the plate.
USDA SR Legacy dry-heat Atlantic cod and haddock. Based on 120 g of cooked edible fish.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: At 120 g cooked, USDA haddock supplies about 2.56 µg vitamin B12, compared with 1.26 µg for Atlantic cod. Both are dry-heat records. These figures compare fish, without batter, breading or tartar sauce.
Match fish and cooking method

If the fillet weighs 85 g cooked, the estimates become 1.81 µg for haddock and 0.89 µg for cod. A single label such as white fish would miss that difference. Identify the species before scaling the portion.
Buyers sometimes see multiple species named cod. The Atlantic cod record is the one used here, and a product label can be a better match for prepared fillets.

article: Does Greek yogurt always have more calcium and B12 than plain yogurt?
Two USDA yogurt entries rank differently for protein, calcium and vitamin B12.
USDA SR Legacy nonfat plain Greek and low-fat plain yogurt references. Independent entries and equal serving size.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: Greek yogurt has more protein and B12 in these two USDA entries, while plain low-fat yogurt has more calcium. A 150 g portion of the Greek reference supplies 15.3 g protein and 165 mg calcium. The plain reference supplies 7.9 g protein and about 275 mg calcium.
Choose a label field before choosing a winner

The samples have different fat categories and production methods, so these rows cannot isolate the effect of straining. Check your own tub if the calcium number matters, especially with a fortified or flavored product.
Track calcium and protein as separate questions. A larger serving of one yogurt will scale every reported nutrient, which can change how the two product portions compare.

article: Which has more thiamin, pork tenderloin or chicken breast?
Compare equal cooked servings before interpreting thiamin per meal.
USDA SR Legacy roasted lean pork tenderloin and roasted chicken breast meat only.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: At 100 g roasted, the USDA lean pork tenderloin lists 0.95 mg thiamin and the chicken breast lists 0.07 mg. Chicken has about 5 g more protein in the same example, so picking a food by protein alone answers a different question.
Compare the portion, not the category

A smaller 70 g tenderloin portion still contributes about 0.67 mg thiamin. That estimate describes lean roasted tenderloin, without any bone or discarded trim, and is not a value for all pork cuts. Marinade and sides would require their own values.
Use this as a way to compare what each ingredient contributes, rather than as a daily goal. A weighed portion makes the contrast easier to reproduce.

article: How much vitamin B5 is in shiitake and white mushrooms?
Scale cooked shiitake and raw white mushrooms to the portions each record describes.
USDA SR Legacy cooked unsalted shiitake and raw white mushroom records. Distinct species and cooking states.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 75 g cooked shiitake side supplies about 2.7 mg pantothenic acid in the USDA entry. A 75 g raw white mushroom portion supplies about 1.1 mg. Matching the weight is useful, but the figures still describe different species and preparations.
Keep the preparation in the comparison

The shiitake entry lists 3.594 mg per 100 g, so 30 g in a rice bowl would provide about 1.08 mg. That is close to the amount in the larger white mushroom serving. The comparison cannot tell you how cooking the same mushrooms would change their B5 concentration.
A dried mushroom weighed before soaking needs a dry reference. Use a cooked weight only when the source represents the prepared food.

article: Which cooked grain base gives more magnesium at the same weight?
Compare quinoa, bulgur and roasted buckwheat at an equal 150 g cooked portion.
USDA SR Legacy cooked quinoa, cooked bulgur and cooked roasted buckwheat groats.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 150 g cooked bowl of quinoa supplies 96 mg magnesium using USDA values. At the same weight, roasted buckwheat groats supply about 77 mg and bulgur 48 mg. Bulgur supplies more fiber than quinoa in these records, so the magnesium order does not carry across to every nutrient.
Three cooked bases with different values

A bowl made with 75 g quinoa and 75 g bulgur has about 72 mg magnesium. Calculate each ingredient separately, then add the two amounts. A packaged blend may have different proportions or ingredients, and its dry weight is a different basis from a cooked bowl.
These are edible cooked weights. Match the food to its preparation before comparing a serving or recording leftovers.

article: Are kidney beans or navy beans higher in potassium and magnesium?
Match drained, cooked 125 g portions and see why the two minerals produce different rankings.
USDA SR Legacy dried mature navy and red kidney beans boiled without salt. Based on equal cooked weights.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: Boiled red kidney beans have slightly more potassium than navy beans in these USDA references. Navy beans have more magnesium. At 125 g, the potassium estimates are close enough that modest portion differences can reverse them.
Pick the mineral you are comparing

If a recipe uses 140 g navy beans instead of 125 g, its bean portion gives about 545 mg potassium. That exceeds the 504 mg in 125 g kidney beans. The navy bean figure also rises to about 74 mg magnesium. The serving can change a close comparison more than the bean name does.
Both references represent boiled unsalted beans. Use the matching canned or salted product if that is what you cooked with.
table: Potassium and magnesium at equal cooked weights

article: How much vitamin D does fortification add to a whole-milk reference?
Read two USDA whole-milk records at a weighed 200 g pour and see the effect of the added vitamin D entry.
USDA SR Legacy whole milk with added vitamin D and whole milk without added vitamins A and D. Weighed basis.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The USDA whole-milk record with added vitamin D gives 2.6 µg for 200 g. The matched-fat record without added vitamins A and D gives 0.2 µg. Both record 3.25% milkfat, so the fat percentage alone cannot identify the vitamin D value.
Read the fortification on your carton

The entries list 1.3 and 0.1 µg per 100 g respectively. The 2.4 µg difference for 200 g is an estimate from these records. It is not a measurement of the amount added to an individual carton. A product elsewhere may follow different fortification rules and use milliliters for its serving.
Look for vitamin D and the serving size on the carton. Use the reference that matches the labeled product.

article: How much sodium do anchovies add to a salad dressing?
Weigh a small portion of drained anchovies and compare a whole recipe with one serving.
USDA SR Legacy European anchovy canned in oil, drained solids. Example dressing uses weighed fish.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: In the USDA drained, oil-packed European anchovy reference, 10 g of fish contributes about 367 mg sodium. Putting that amount into dressing for four equal servings gives about 92 mg from the anchovy per serving.
Measure the anchovy before blending

Make the comparison before including salt, cheese and a prepared dressing base. Five grams of this anchovy entry gives about 183 mg sodium, half the amount from 10 g. The Nutrition Facts on a specific tin is more suitable if its cure and serving size differ.
Drain and weigh the fish you use. The per-100 g value applies to solids and cannot separately estimate the sodium in packing liquid or anything left in the tin.

article: Does ground flax add more thiamin than chia at the same weight?
Compare two 10 g seed portions using the reported USDA thiamin values.
USDA SR Legacy flaxseed and dried chia. Estimates represent seed ingredients without additives.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: At 10 g each, flaxseed gives about 0.164 mg thiamin and dried chia gives 0.062 mg in the USDA references. The numbers compare the same seed weight. Scoops with the same volume can hold different gram amounts, especially when one ingredient is ground.
Compare tablespoons by weight if you measure the topping

For breakfast with 6 g flax and 6 g chia, the estimated total is around 0.136 mg. Repeating this calculation from the actual gram amounts makes it easier to compare different spoon sizes. The reference flaxseed describes the seed itself and does not account for mixing it with anything.
Use the ingredient’s own label or a matching plain seed reference. This table describes what is added to the bowl, before the base is counted.
table: Thiamin from equal amounts of seed

article: How much folate is in a mango and avocado salsa?
Build a 150 g example and measure the change when you reverse the two ingredients’ proportions.
USDA SR Legacy raw mango and all commercial varieties of raw avocado. Example excludes other ingredients.
copy: A salsa with 100 g mango flesh and 50 g avocado flesh has about 84 µg folate before other ingredients. Swapping those weights gives about 103 µg without changing the 150 g total. The result changes because avocado has a higher value per gram in these entries.
Hold the finished weight steady

The estimates use 43 µg folate per 100 g mango and 81 µg per 100 g avocado. If you make the first version and eat one-third of the batch, you get about 28 µg from those two ingredients. Keeping the two ratio calculations separate avoids logging the heavier ingredient twice.
This is a fresh-flesh reference. Use a matching source if a prepared salsa has additional ingredients or canned fruit.

article: How much folate is in 75 g of leek before or after cooking?
Compare raw and boiled leek food records and work out why matching grams cannot measure retention.
USDA SR Legacy raw and boiled drained leek bulb and lower leaf portion. Separate records.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: A 75 g portion of raw leek gives about 48 µg folate, while the USDA boiled, drained leek reference gives 18 µg at the same weight. These numbers help you choose a reference. They cannot tell you exactly what happened to folate when you cooked one leek.
Do not treat the two weights as the same batch

A retention test would measure the raw starting amount, cooked yield and nutrients in the edible outcome. If you use the boiling liquid for soup, a drained reference by itself does not describe what the liquid contains. For a bowl of plain drained cooked leek, weigh the portion and use the cooked row.
The named records cover the bulb and lower leaf portion. Discarded green tops should not be included in the weighed portion unless actually used.

article: How much calcium is in the sesame seeds sprinkled on rice?
Scale whole dried sesame seed calcium to 3, 6 and 12 g amounts.
USDA SR Legacy whole dried sesame seeds, including the hull where applicable to the entry.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: Whole dried sesame seeds have 975 mg calcium per 100 g in the USDA entry. A 6 g sprinkle has about 59 mg. The per-100 g value looks large because it describes much more seed than you would normally weigh for this topping.
Keep the whole-seed basis

Use 9.75 mg calcium per gram to calculate a weighed amount. A 12 g batch split between four bowls contributes about 29 mg to each bowl. This calculation describes the calcium present in whole seeds. A hulled seed, sesame paste or mixed seasoning needs its own entry or label.
Count the actual serving of rice separately. The values here deliberately isolate the topping and keep its role in the meal visible.

article: How much phosphorus is in trout, salmon and cod at dinner?
Match the dry-heat cooked weight in three USDA fish records.
USDA SR Legacy dry-heat cooked farmed rainbow trout, farmed Atlantic salmon and Atlantic cod.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: A 110 g cooked portion provides about 297 mg phosphorus in the rainbow trout reference, 277 mg in the Atlantic salmon entry and 152 mg in the Atlantic cod entry. These are total phosphorus in the fish references.
Compare unseasoned references separately from prepared products

Prepared foods can have added ingredients, and a nutrition label may leave phosphorus amounts off. Check the ingredient list for preparation details and use a measured source for any quantitative comparison. Do not assign this cod estimate to every breaded fish product.
These estimates scale the cooked edible fish and leave off sauce, batter and cooking additions. The small trout-to-salmon difference can move if the served pieces have different weights.
table: Phosphorus in 110 g of three cooked fish

article: Do walnuts or cashews provide more zinc and copper in a handful?
Compare equal 28 g portions and calculate how a half-and-half mix changes the minerals.
USDA SR Legacy English walnuts and raw cashews. No coatings or seasonings.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: An example 28 g handful of raw cashews supplies about 1.62 mg zinc and 0.61 mg copper. English walnuts at the same weight give about 0.87 mg zinc and 0.44 mg copper. A mix of the two lands between these results for both minerals.
Scale each nut in the mix

If the pack is half each by weight, add the contribution from 14 g cashews and 14 g walnuts. That yields about 1.24 mg zinc and 0.53 mg copper. Counting the same number of nuts can give a different ratio because the individual pieces need not weigh the same.
Flavors and coatings change the weight of a snack. The reference here uses the nut itself.
table: Mineral estimates for 28 g snack portions

article: Does the fish with more protein also give more vitamin B6?
Compare 100 g tilapia and Atlantic salmon using USDA dry-heat references.
USDA SR Legacy cooked tilapia and farmed Atlantic salmon. Compared at equal cooked weight.
related: Compare reference foods in the nutrient explorer
copy: Cooked tilapia has about 26.2 g protein per 100 g in the USDA reference, compared with 22.1 g for farmed Atlantic salmon. The vitamin B6 order goes the other way. Salmon lists 0.647 mg B6 and tilapia lists 0.123 mg for that weight.
Keep the two nutrient rankings separate

For an 85 g salmon portion, the estimate is about 0.55 mg B6. It takes a much larger weight of the tilapia reference to give the same value. That arithmetic explains why an entry chosen just for its protein can miss a micronutrient difference.
Use a species- and preparation-matched entry when logging a fish. Coating, sauce and the cooked serving’s weight can alter the finished meal comparison.
